analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for misclassified 'independent contractors' to be recognized as employees with benefits and protections.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Obama with three co-sponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2007 and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that treat workers as 'independent contractors' avoid paying employment taxes, unemployment insurance, and providing minimum wage, overtime, and benefit protections. This bill would let a worker petition the Treasury Department to rule on their status, and once a determination found they were really an employee, the company would have to treat them as an employee from then on. It would also repeal a special tax 'safe harbor' that shields employers from IRS reclassification even after a finding of misclassification, end a ban on the IRS issuing rules on contractor status, and order the Treasury and Labor Departments to share information and investigate industries with high misclassification rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are misclassified as independent contractors gain the ability to force a ruling on their status and, if reclassified, receive employment tax treatment, plus the wage, hour, and benefit protections that attach to employees. The bill adds attorney-fee awards and bans retaliation against workers who petition. Treasury also recovers employment taxes employers currently avoid.

how_it_helps.text: Any worker could petition the Treasury Department for a determination of whether they are an employee or contractor, with a ruling required within 90 days for transient or seasonal industries like construction, and an administrative appeal if they lose.
Once Treasury finds a worker was misclassified, the employer must treat that worker as an employee for employment taxes going forward; the existing Section 530 safe harbor no longer shields them.

The bill repeals the 1978 provision that bans the IRS from issuing regulations or rulings on contractor classification, and eliminates the 'industry practice' defense as a basis for claiming the safe harbor.

Workers who win reclassification can recover attorney and expert witness fees from the employer, and employers may not fire, refuse to contract with, or otherwise retaliate against a worker for filing a petition.

Treasury must audit employers found to have misclassified workers, tell the Labor Department, notify workers of any self-employment tax refund due, and the two departments must exchange information, issue annual reports, and investigate industries with misclassification problems.

Employers must tell independent contractors at hire which labor and employment protections do not apply to them and that they can seek an IRS status determination, and must keep a three-year list of their contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that currently classify workers as contractors would owe employment taxes, unemployment insurance contributions, and the cost of benefits and wage protections, plus new notice and recordkeeping duties. Industries with high misclassification rates face Treasury audits and Labor Department investigations. Taxpayers fund the new Treasury and Labor enforcement staff.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new paperwork on every employer that uses contractors: a written notice at hire and a three-year list of contractors with names, addresses, and Social Security numbers that must be available for inspection.
It opens the door to Treasury employment tax audits and Department of Labor investigations for entire industries, which businesses would bear whether or not their own classifications were improper.

Some workers genuinely prefer contractor status, because self-employed people can deduct business expenses against self-employment tax; the bill's notice requirements and reclassification machinery could push willing contractors into employee treatment they did not want.
Enforcement is funded with an open-ended authorization of 'such sums as are necessary' for Treasury and Labor, a cost borne by general taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: misclassification leaves workers without unemployment insurance, minimum wage, and overtime protections while shifting tax obligations onto them, and the bill builds a direct remedy with fees, retaliation protection, and agency enforcement. The costs are paperwork, audit exposure, and new agency spending, and some legitimate contractor arrangements could be swept in. The design is aimed at clearing away 1978-era shields, the safe harbor after a misclassification finding and the ban on IRS rules, rather than banning contracting, so the burden falls mainly on employers whose classifications do not hold up.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to its Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Obama introduced the bill on September 12, 2007, joined by Senators Durbin, Kennedy, and Murray.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day.
The bill picked up six Democratic co-sponsors.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use the independent-contractor label avoided employment taxes, unemployment insurance costs, and wage-and-hour protections, and continued doing so for the rest of the Congress; misclassified workers got nothing.

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Dick Durbin, Ted Kennedy, and Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senators (D-IL, D-MA, D-WA), original co-sponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined Senator Obama as original co-sponsors on introduction.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill; the record shows no committee action after the September 2007 referral.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it had no path to a vote without committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters, the sponsor and six co-sponsors, were Democrats; the record shows no Republican support, and the Finance Committee, chaired by a Democrat, never acted on it.

industries.industry: Employers that misclassify workers as independent contractors (construction, trucking, janitorial, and similar industries)
industries.note: These employers avoid employment taxes, unemployment insurance, and wage-and-hour obligations by classifying workers as contractors. The bill removes their safe harbor after a misclassification finding, requires audits, and lets workers force the issue, so their savings came directly out of workers' protections.

industries.industry: Professional employer organizations and staffing/outsourcing firms built on 1099 arrangements
industries.note: Their business model depends on the contractor classification the bill targets; the repeal of the ban on IRS classification rules and the 'industry practice' defense would have narrowed the shield they rely on.

industries.industry: Businesses that use contractors in good faith
industries.note: Compliant businesses face new notice duties and a three-year contractor list with workers' Social Security numbers, and lose the 'industry practice' safe-harbor defense, but could keep lawful contractor arrangements.

industries.industry: The Treasury and federal workforce enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill authorizes open-ended funding for IRS and Labor Department enforcement and gives them petition, audit, and information-sharing powers, so misclassification becomes easier to police.
